stories.headline: In reversal, Chargers not placing Charlie Kolar (forearm) on IR
stories.summary: In a surprising reversal, the Chargers are not placing tight end Charlie Kolar on injured reserve after he injured his left forearm in Sunday's game.
stories.body:
EL SEGUNDO, Calif. -- In a surprising reversal, the Los Angeles Chargers are not placing tight end Charlie Kolar on injured reserve after he injured his left forearm in Sunday's 26-14 loss to the Las Vegas Raiders.

Coach Jim Harbaugh said Monday that Kolar would go on injured reserve along with tight end David Njoku, but Kolar's surgery Monday changed his prognosis, and he will remain on the active roster.

Still, Harbaugh said Wednesday that Kolar won't play Sunday against the Buffalo Bills, or practice Wednesday.

With just one healthy tight end on the active roster in Oronde Gadsden, the Chargers signed tight end Hayden Rucci on Tuesday, poaching him from Jacksonville's practice squad.

Rucci is familiar with this Chargers system, having played four games in Miami last season under Mike McDaniel, now offensive coordinator for the Chargers.

Rucci will likely be ready to contribute as early as Sunday and could be a big help in getting Los Angeles' struggling offense back on track. Gadsden struggles as a run blocker, which puts the offense at a significant disadvantage. Having Rucci, who is already familiar with the system and thrives as a blocker, gives this offense some hope to be multidimensional.

stories.headline: Sources: Extension unlikely as Knicks, Karl-Anthony Towns talks stall
stories.summary: Extension talks have stagnated between the Knicks and Karl-Anthony Towns, and an agreement is considered unlikely as the team begins camp, sources told ESPN.
stories.body:
Talks have stagnated between the New York Knicks and Karl-Anthony Towns on a contract extension, and an agreement is considered unlikely as the team begins training camp next week, sources told ESPN on Wednesday.

The sides have spent extensive time discussing a potential extension during the offseason, but there has been no movement lately in negotiations, sources said, as the Knicks stand to go for a repeat following their first NBA title in 53 years.

Towns, who will turn 31 in mid-November, is eligible to receive a contract extension for up to four years and $273 million, according to ESPN's Bobby Marks.

An All-Star in his two seasons in New York, Towns averaged 15.9 points, 10.6 rebounds and 4.9 assists on 55% shooting through last season's playoffs, helping the Knicks to a 16-3 mark as they defeated the San Antonio Spurs in five games in the NBA Finals.

Knicks owner James Dolan has repeatedly said he wanted to keep the Knicks out of the punitive second apron. Valuable backup center Mitchell Robinson was one of the casualties of the edict, as he signed with the Boston Celtics this offseason.

Towns is due $57 million this season and has a $61 million player option for 2027-28. As it stands, the Knicks and Towns could come to an agreement at any point this season, but it is not imminent and appears unlikely in the short-term.

The Knicks have many looming contract decisions over the next several months. Swingman Josh Hart is eligible for a contract extension as well, while Jalen Brunson and OG Anunoby will be eligible for contract extensions next offseason.

stories.headline: Lewis Hamilton on F1 races becoming shorter in 2027: 'Makes no sense'
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton has criticized plans to make grands prix 15 kilometres shorter next year, saying it "makes absolutely no sense."
stories.body:
Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton has criticized plans to make grands prix 15 kilometres shorter next year, saying it "makes absolutely no sense."

In 2027, Formula 1 races will be two or three laps shorter (depending on the length of the circuit) due to changes to the engine regulations that will result in higher rates of fuel consumption.

In order to avoid teams investing in costly chassis redesigns to accommodate larger fuel tanks, the FIA announced last week that it would shorten races from 305km to 290km.

"The races should be longer because they are physically easier than ever before," Hamilton was quoted by the Press Association ahead of this weekend's Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

"This is supposed to be a sport which is the most physically and mentally demanding, and there are some where you are on the edge.

"But that is where you want to see -- athletes right on the edge of performance and pushing their bodies further, pushing the levels and pushing the boundaries. Shortening the races makes absolutely no sense to me."

The shortening of races stems from complaints made by drivers about this year's hybrid engine regulations, which initially targeted a 50/50 split between internal combustion power and battery power.

The notional 50/50 split proved to be closer to 53/47 in favour of the internal combustion engine, but the regulations still resulted in cars that regularly run out of electric power around circuits where energy deployment is high and energy harvesting is limited.

For next year, the rules have been tweaked to achieve a 58/42 split -- which will become 60/40 in 2028 -- but in order to increase the power output of the internal combustion engine, it will need to consume more fuel.

Accommodating the extra fuel needed to complete a 305km race distance under the tweaked regulations would have required teams to make costly redesigns to their chassis, so the FIA reduced the length of the race by 15km to allow them continue with the existing fuel tank size.

- Alpine's Pierre Gasly warns against 'disturbing' threats after teammate Franco Colapinto incident

- Fernando Alonso highlights ongoing talks with F1 bosses around rules: 'Circuits were killed'

Hamilton admitted he had not been briefed on the reasons for the changes, but is concerned the shortening of races will reduce the physical challenge and limit tyre strategy options.

"I don't really know anything about it or any of the reasons they put it up behind it," he added.

"I think the races should be longer because the races are physically easier than ever before.

"So shortening, I don't think, makes much sense. If you think about this weekend, we have the C3, 4, 5 [tyre compounds] that can pretty much all do the race distance.

"So we have a lot of races where it's only a one stop. It's not particularly challenging.

"So for me, there's been many races where I wish we had more laps. It's the opposite that I would be asking for [which] is longer races, to be honest."

stories.headline: Man United selling chunks of Old Trafford pitch
stories.summary: Old Trafford -- the home of Manchester United -- has seen plenty of history over the years. Now, fans can own a piece of the pitch ...for £125 ($165).
stories.body:
Old Trafford -- the home of Manchester United -- has seen plenty of history over the years. Now, fans can own a piece of the pitch ...for £125 ($165).

The hallowed stadium has witnessed countless victories -- particularly during the Sir Alex Ferguson era, in which United won 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League trophies, and numerous FA Cup triumphs.

The club is selling chunks of the ground off.

Old Trafford has borne witness to some of United's worst moments, too, including a 5-0 defeat to bitter rivals Liverpool, a 6-1 loss to Tottenham and, most recently, a capitulation against Brighton in the Carabao Cup -- in which the Red Devils let a 2-0 lead slip and fell to a 3-2 defeat.

The loss to Brighton marked the first time in 42 years that United had lost a match at home when leading at half-time.

According to club media, the pitch was completely dug up and stripped back to its foundation in June -- for the first time in 14 years -- and sections of it were preserved and then placed into glass cubes.

On their website, United said the digging up of the pitch was completed by groundsperson Tony Sinclair and was done to regrow the surface in order to "improve player welfare and water drainage."

United fans may be hoping that their season will soon improve along with the pitch.

stories.headline: Are the New York Liberty a real WNBA championship contender?
stories.summary: After an inconsistent regular season, New York will have to hit the road in the WNBA playoffs.
stories.body:
NEW YORK -- The 30-year history of the New York Liberty has featured twists and turns, heartache and highs and, at times, even down-right irrelevance. But Liberty faithful have come to expect that with the arrival of autumn comes the arrival of playoff basketball in Brooklyn and, ideally, a championship.

Yet before the postseason opens Sunday, the Atlanta Dream are in town during the first week of fall for two games in three days to close the regular season, a playoff teaser as both teams vie for better seeding and momentum.

"You can feel it in the building. You can feel it on the streets outside of Barclays," first-year Liberty coach Chris DeMarco said Monday of the franchise's championship culture. "It's a passionate fanbase, and the standard has been winning, and it starts with our stars and our All-Stars, our top players, and what's expected out of them time and time again in a city that loves sports and a city that loves basketball.

"I couldn't be more excited to be here right now in this position where we're getting closer to the playoffs."

Four hours later, the Liberty walked off their home court with a 95-84 loss, the result officially knocking them out of contention for a top-four seed and home-court advantage for the first round.

To win a championship, they'll have to do it the hard way. Just as much of this season has been.

Between returning their big three and signing Satou Sabally in free agency, the Liberty were, as they have been since Breanna Stewart and Jonquel Jones arrived, considered championship contenders entering the season. Though DeMarco was new, the experience and talent on the roster in May made New York look well-positioned to ensure its 2025 first-round playoff exit following back-to-back Finals appearances was a mere blip.

Yet a roller-coaster season has put into question whether that will be the case. Between a rash of injuries, inconsistent play and a 13-12 start that Stewart described as a "what the f---" moment, the Liberty's performance has evoked questions about whether or why they haven't always played to their potential.

New York will enter the playoffs buoyed by a strong regular-season finish the team says more accurately reflects what it is capable of. Amid the ups and downs, the Liberty have maintained they have the players to win a second WNBA championship in three years.

When the playoffs tip off Sunday, the Liberty will be out to show who they really are. And the league will be watching to see what happens next if a franchise with perhaps the highest internal expectations once more falls short of a deep playoff run.

"We know this team has been through a lot," Stewart said in late August, "but we have a lot of fight left in us."

ONE YEAR AGO, the Liberty made shockwaves when they announced they were moving on from Sandy Brondello, the winningest coach in franchise history who'd guided New York to its first WNBA title 11 months earlier.

At the time -- days after New York had lost in the first round -- general manager Jonathan Kolb described the decision as an effort to pursue "evolution and innovation," to "keep pushing the New York Liberty to new heights" and "position ourselves to be at the top of the league in a real sustainable way."

"We need to nail this," Kolb told reporters regarding his next hire. "If we're going to make a bold decision like this, our players deserve to get the best."

The Liberty hired DeMarco in December, well after the league's other coaching vacancies had been filled. The latest NBA-assistant-turned-WNBA head coach, DeMarco was on the Golden State Warriors staff for their four recent titles; his head coaching experience came from leading the Bahamas men's national team over the previous six years.

In the preseason, players spoke of embracing a new era and expressed enthusiasm for DeMarco's new offense, which they touted for its simplicity and clarity. But things got off to a rocky start. After a 20-point road loss against the Indiana Fever on July 18, New York was 13-12.

"I'm surprised at how the first half of the season went from a record standpoint," said Stewart, who hasn't flirted with a .500 record since 2017, her second year in the league. "I was like, 'What the f---? Like, you gotta be f---ing kidding me.'"

Injuries piled up. Sabrina Ionescu played one game in the first five weeks of this season. Sabally made only 13 appearances before being ruled out for the season as she dealt with the effects of a second concussion in eight months. Leonie Fiebich, a critical cog to the Liberty's defense, was sidelined by a foot injury for seven weeks in July and August and has been available for only 20 games.

Then Betnijah Laney-Hamilton -- who sat out all of 2025 because of a knee injury -- fell out of the rotation entirely, picking up DNPs for three weeks before being waived four days after the trade deadline. It was an emotional departure internally for one of the Liberty's longest-tenured players and a 2024 champion who was viewed as the embodiment of New York grit. The prolonged nature of the ordeal and lack of clarity over why she'd been relegated also frustrated the fanbase, with DeMarco getting booed during introductions ahead of the first game following her release. "Welcome to New York," Stewart interjected when DeMarco was asked about it.

Consistency was also hard to come by, not only game to game but sometimes within a game. The Liberty went 16-6 this season against teams below .500, the worst such record among playoff teams. DeMarco and players acknowledged they needed to be better at playing a full 40 minutes and refocusing quicker when things didn't go their way, and that sometimes not making shots affected their defensive effort.

Things reached Jekyll-and-Hyde proportions when New York won eight straight games across late May and June but then lost eight of its next 10, not including clinching their second Commissioner's Cup championship.

The team held multiple meetings after the initial loss to Indiana, including one postgame in the locker room with players only and another the following day with the entire group. They discussed the importance of each person remembering what got them there and, from the coaching staff down to the players riding the bench, that they were all in it together and it would take everyone to be successful.

"You can sit in the locker room and feel sorry for yourself and complain and be upset about the way things are going, or you can do something about it," Ionescu said. "And I think we all kind of took it upon ourselves to try and do something about it."

The Liberty focused on stacking wins even if they weren't pretty. They learned to embrace that it was OK if things were more difficult for the time being, as long as they could play their best basketball by the playoffs.

"We had this expectation of being one of the better teams in the league and being maybe top two, top three, whatever it is, and that wasn't really materializing for us at the beginning of the season," Jones said in August. "We put a lot of pressure on ourselves, and I think that pressure turned into anxiety, and then it turned into the way that we were playing on the court, where we just weren't really moving the ball, everybody was just trying to figure it out, but we were all trying to figure it out separately."

New York is 13-5 since that July 18 loss, and in that span boasts the second-best offensive rating in the league at 114.3 points per 100 possessions. The other end of the court has been a work in progress all season. The Liberty rank seventh in defensive rating and have struggled to guard the 3-point line.

"We're an offensive powerhouse ... and everyone knows that," forward Rebecca Allen said. "The question mark people have is, 'Defensively, can they rise to that challenge?' I think that we've really put that question on ourselves as well, and we're taking it quite personally."

DeMarco acknowledged the changes in personnel availability from game to game forced the coaching staff to continuously pivot and sometimes reinvent the lineup -- all as he was navigating the learning curve that comes with being a first-time coach in the WNBA.

"You've been able to see it through our record over the last month," Ionescu said Monday of DeMarco's progression. "Obviously, he's learning the league a lot more and understanding what it takes to be a head coach in this league, and he's had to adapt and adjust really quickly. And I think he's done a great job."

Having more continuity in the lineup has helped, Ionescu added, as has Fiebich's return over the past six games. The Liberty are 12-11 without Fiebich and 14-6 with her.

"I don't know if we proved anything to ourselves," Stewart said after Fiebich's first game back on Aug. 22, a 109-102 win at home over the Fever. "Now I'm really excited for us to continue to build. Like, better late than never, I guess.

"Now it's just really important how we finish this season."

THE DREAM'S THREE-POINT halftime lead Monday suddenly ballooned to 10 not even 2 minutes, 30 seconds into the third quarter, prompting a Liberty timeout. New York hung around, even cutting the deficit to two, but Atlanta's third-quarter punch in which the Dream scored 32 points and capitalized on a slew of Liberty turnovers proved the difference.

New York will enter the postseason with recent quality wins over the Fever and Minnesota Lynx, and gets another shot at Atlanta on Wednesday. But the team is not yet a finished product. Keeping composure amid an opposing team's run -- what players have acknowledged has been an issue throughout the season -- will be even more critical in the playoffs.

"We have shown what we can do, but we have to do it consistently," guard Rebekah Gardner said Monday. "That's going to be the difference in how far we go in the postseason."

New York has championship experience, but bookmakers and historical precedent are not in its favor. DraftKings gives them the sixth-longest odds at 14-1 to win the 2026 title, better than only the Washington Mystics and Dallas Wings. The lowest-seeded team to win a WNBA title was the No. 6 Chicago Sky in 2021, also the only team to win a championship without finishing top four in the standings.

The Liberty's 10-11 record against playoff teams this season is tied with the Dream and Mystics for fourth best, slotted behind the Lynx, Golden State Valkyries and Las Vegas Aces. Even in its 13-5 run since dropping to 13-12, the team's 6.3 net rating ranks sixth in the league, ahead of only the Lynx and Wings in that stretch.

Even still, few teams probably would line up to face the Liberty in the first round. Their core four of Ionescu, Stewart, Jones and Fiebich has chemistry, shared bond and a collective will to win, Ionescu said, forged from their 2024 championship and the adversity that has come along the way.

"I think everyone knows we're not a traditional [low] seed," Ionescu said in early August. "At least for me personally, it's less worrying about the seed that we are because I know when we're playing our best, we can beat anyone, even if we are an 8-seed."

They also have Stewart, who in 2026 has further solidified herself as the sport's greatest winner with Unrivaled, EuroLeague, Commissioner's Cup and World Cup championships. She nearly willed the Liberty to the semifinals on a sprained MCL last year and is playing with the same determination and heightened leadership down the stretch of this season.

"I'm really locked in," Stewart said Monday. "I know that the moment is almost here as far as what we want to do in playoffs, and knowing that Wednesday is our last get-right game before we figure out where we go and who we play and vice versa.

"I just want to leave it all on the court and do that on a nightly basis. And I think that making sure to set the tone for my team and really let them know what type of basketball we're going to be playing for the next hopefully month and beyond."

ESPN Research contributed to this report.

stories.headline: The performance bonuses for Van, Tsarukyan? Spots in P4P top 10
stories.summary: Former UFC champion puts elite status of women's flyweight division on display in ESPN's P4P top 10.
stories.body:
UFC 331 delivered some remarkable performances, a couple of which landed fighters in the ESPN pound-for-pound rankings.

One of them is not heavyweight Sean Sharaf, despite him pulling off the biggest upset in UFC history with his 12-second knockout of mega-prospect Gable Steveson. Women's flyweight Casey O'Neill produced a leading candidate for submission of the year, escaping a dangerous position to quickly armbar Eduarda Moura, but that didn't earn O'Neill a top-10 spot, either.

Both of those fighters were eye openers, but the rankings were reserved for the two winners of Saturday's headline fights.

In the main event, Joshua Van successfully defended his men's flyweight title against former champion Alexandre Pantoja, using crisp boxing and efficient grappling to secure a unanimous decision. Van moves into the men's rankings at No. 8, and Pantoja, who previously occupied that position, drops out.

Also earning a top-10 spot is co-main event winner Arman Tsarukyan, who knocked out flashy striker Mauricio Ruffy to all but secure a lightweight title shot. Tsarukyan moves in at No. 10, with former light heavyweight champion Alex Pereira falling from the rankings.

For the ESPN divisional MMA rankings, click here.

Note: Results are current; rankings are as of Sept. 23. To be eligible for the rankings, a fighter must have competed over the past 12 months or must have an upcoming fight booked. Fighters who have been dropped for inactivity can be reinstated only after they compete.

Men's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Islam Makhachev

UFC welterweight champion

Record: 29-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Ian Machado Garry, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Makhachev vacated the UFC lightweight championship to go for a second title at welterweight. By winning that belt last November with a thrashing of Jack Della Maddalena, Makhachev staked his place among MMA's greatest -- not just in today's sport but of all time. His win over Machado Garry at UFC 330 was his 17th straight, breaking the UFC record for consecutive wins. Makhachev is piling up unprecedented achievements.

2. Petr Yan

UFC bantamweight champion

Record: 20-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Merab Dvalishvili, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Dvalishvili

What a return to the top it's been for Yan. He began his career with 15 consecutive wins before going on a 1-4 run from 2021 to 2023. That almost doesn't feel real now, after watching him reclaim his throne against Dvalishvili, who once handed him the worst loss of his career. Yan took a major detour, but this was the destination we felt he was capable of before the skid. He once again looks like one of the best fighters on the planet. He can prove it by beating Dvalishvili again.

3. Merab Dvalishvili

UFC bantamweight

Record: 21-5

Last: L (UD) vs. Petr Yan, Dec. 6, 2025

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Yan

Dvalishvili was on one of the most impressive runs through the UFC's bantamweight division ever. Not only did he defeat Sean O'Malley for the second time in nine months at UFC 316, but he showcased a new part of his game, finishing O'Malley with a guillotine. Starting in August 2022, Dvalishvili beat José Aldo, Yan, Henry Cejudo, O'Malley (twice), Umar Nurmagomedov and Cory Sandhagen. But at UFC 323, in an attempt to become the first champion in UFC history to successfully defend a title four times in a calendar year, Dvalishvili lost a rematch with Yan. They will fight for a third time at UFC 333.

T-4. Tom Aspinall

UFC heavyweight

Record: 15-3, 1 NC

Last: NC1 vs. Ciryl Gane, Oct. 25, 2025

Next: TBA

You can make a case that Aspinall is the most dynamic, skillful, talented heavyweight the sport has seen. He is dominating opponents in a way that is unmatched. No one can last a round with him. He had hoped to prove his supremacy against Jon Jones, but Jones opted to retire, elevating Aspinall from interim champion. His first defense of the undisputed belt ended anticlimactically, as an eye poke resulted in his UFC 321 fight with Gane being declared a no-contest. Still recovering from the eye injury, Aspinall vacated his title on Sept. 14.

T-4. Justin Gaethje

UFC lightweight champion

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 28-5

Last: W (TKO4) vs. Ilia Topuria, June 14

Next: TBA

Gaethje has spent his 15-year career thrilling MMA fans, but before the title bout on the White House lawn, all he had to show for it -- aside from 15 bonus checks in 15 UFC appearances -- were two missed opportunities to be an undisputed champion. His fourth-round TKO of Topuria got Gaethje over the hump. It was a resilient performance in a back-and-forth battle that is a prime candidate for fight of the year. More important for Gaethje: At age 37, he is finally sitting at the top of the mountain.

6. Ilia Topuria

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: 5

Record: 17-1

Last: L (TKO4) vs. Justin Gaethje, June 14

Next: TBA

Topuria was an undefeated two-division champion when he ran into Gaethje at UFC Freedom 250 and was brutalized in a stoppage loss. How will that affect the immediate future of Topuria? His knockout wins over two of the greatest featherweights, Alexander Volkanovski and Max Holloway, gave him an intimidating aura. Can the former champion get that back?

7. Alexander Volkanovski

UFC featherweight champion

Record: 28-4

Last: W (UD) vs. Diego Lopes, Jan. 31

Next: Oct. 24 vs. Movsar Evloev

It felt as if the sport had started to write Volkanovski's eulogy following his knockout loss to Ilia Topuria in February 2024. Volkanovski noticed and made a point of proving to everyone he still has plenty left by recapturing the featherweight belt at UFC 314, the first of two consecutive wins over Lopes. His age (37) will likely continue to be a prefight topic, which is fine because Volkanovski enjoys proving people wrong. Can he hand Evloev his first loss at UFC 333?

8. Joshua Van

UFC flyweight champion

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 18-2

Last: W (UD) vs. Alexandre Pantoja, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Van has been champion since December, but until UFC 331, there were doubters. Van had been handed the belt by default, when his challenge for the title was waved off after 26 seconds because Pantoja dislocated his left elbow. Van went on to defend the title against Tatsuro Taira in May, then faced Pantoja in a rematch this past weekend. Van produced a clear victory -- his eighth win in a row -- to leave no doubt who rules at 125 pounds.

9. Ciryl Gane

UFC heavyweight champion

Record: 14-2, 1 NC

Last: W (TKO2) vs. Alex Pereira, June 14

Next: Nov. 14 vs. Josh Hokit

Gane is unique in that he is the first -- and could very well go down as the only -- heavyweight to face the division's four biggest names in Francis Ngannou, Jon Jones, Tom Aspinall and Pereira. None of those four have fought each other, yet all four have have fought the Frenchman. Gane was 0-2 with a no-contest against that group before he knocked out Pereira in the second round of their interim title fight. Gane was elevated to undisputed champ after Aspinall, still injured, vacated his title, and the new champ will defend against Hokit at UFC 334.

10. Arman Tsarukyan

UFC lightweight

Previous ranking: Unranked

Record: 24-3

Last: W (KO1) vs. Mauricio Ruffy, Sept. 19

Next: TBA

Tsarukyan is right back in the place he was in January 2025 -- on the cusp of a title fight. He withdrew from that challenge of Islam Makhachev one day before UFC 311 because of a back injury, and later in the year he was passed over twice when the UFC was booking lightweight title bouts. But by knocking out Mauricio Ruffy with an elbow in the first round at UFC 331, Tsarukyan put himself back at the front of the line.

Other fighter receiving votes: Alex Pereira.

How our panel voted

Women's pound-for-pound rankings

1. Valentina Shevchenko

UFC flyweight

Record: 26-4-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Zhang Weili, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

Shevchenko's dominance came under question in 2022 and 2023, when she went 1-1-1 in a trilogy with Alexa Grasso. Boy, does that feel like a long time ago now. Shevchenko more than reasserted herself as the best flyweight in the world, and then she established herself as the No. 1 woman in the world, period. It wasn't surprising that she beat Zhang, but it was surprising how easy she made it look. Shevchenko is out injured, however, so she has vacated her UFC title, which will be up for grabs when Natalia Silva meets Wang Cong on Oct. 3.

2. Zhang Weili

UFC flyweight / strawweight

Record: 26-4

Last: L (UD) vs. Valentina Shevchenko, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: TBA

It's hard to move up in weight, especially at the highest level. That sounds like it should be obvious, but Zhang had been dominant at 115 pounds for so long, some of us might have taken for granted how big of a challenge moving to 125 would be. UFC 322 was a bad night for Zhang, but she doesn't have many. And if she decides to stay at flyweight, it certainly seems reasonable to believe she'll fare better in the future.

3. Cris Cyborg

PFL featherweight champion

Record: 30-2, 1 NC

Last: W (UD) vs. Ketlen Vieira, Aug. 22

Next: TBA

It had been a while since Cyborg had fought an elite opponent in MMA until she met Larissa Pacheco in 2024. That was a legitimate matchup -- and many within the industry were predicting Cyborg's downfall. Instead, she took out the PFL's two-weight champion, upending all of Pacheco's momentum. One of the original pioneers of women's MMA is once again a champion after getting her second career submission at PFL Lyon in December. The PFL promoted her fight with Vieira as a retirement bout, but after her win Cyborg did not sound like someone who is done fighting.

4. Mackenzie Dern

UFC strawweight champion

Record: 17-5

Last: W (UD) vs. Gillian Robertson, Aug. 15

Next: TBA

Dern's rise to the 115-pound throne was truly a changing of the guard. She is the division's first first-time champion since 2019, because the previous three champs -- Zhang Weili, Carla Esparza and Rose Namajunas -- all were in their second reigns. Dern, nearly a decade into her MMA career after multiple jiu-jitsu world championships, has won four fights in a row, including a dominant performance against a fellow grappling-heavy fighter, Robertson, in her first title defense.

5. Natalia Silva

UFC flyweight

Record: 20-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Rose Namajunas, Jan. 24

Next: Oct. 3 vs. Wang Cong

Silva is looking every bit the part of a future UFC champion following a dominant display against Alexa Grasso at UFC 315 and a victory over Namajunas at UFC 324. Silva's stick-and-move style has frustrated even the highest level of opponent, and she's got youth on her side as she won't turn 30 until 2027. With an injured Valentina Shevchenko having vacated the title, Silva will fight Wang for the belt at UFC 332.

6. Alexa Grasso

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 10

Record: 18-5-1

Last: W (UD) vs. Manon Fiorot, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Grasso went nearly three years without winning a fight, but her 2023 win right before the skid was a huge one, a submission of Valentina Shevchenko for the UFC title. What followed were two more fights with Shevchenko -- a draw, then a loss -- and then a loss to Natalia Silva. But she reasserted herself with a finish of Maycee Barber in March, then got the best of Fiorot, a fellow title contender, at Noche UFC to put herself in position for another title shot.

7. Dakota Ditcheva

PFL flyweight

Record: 16-0

Last: W (UD) vs. Denise Kielholtz, July 31

Next: TBA

Not only did Ditcheva win the PFL's flyweight season in 2024, but she did so in spectacular fashion -- a TKO finish over Taila Santos, who once challenged for a UFC title. Ditcheva fought only once in 2025, dominating Sumiko Inaba in the co-main event of the first PFL Champions Series card in Cape Town, South Africa. She then spent over a year on the sideline, healing injuries to both hands, before returning at PFL New York with a dominant win over Kielholtz.

8. Manon Fiorot

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 6

Record: 13-3

Last: L (UD) vs. Alexa Grasso, Sept. 12

Next: TBA

Fiorot had handled everyone the UFC put in front of her -- except the champion, Valentina Shevchenko, who defeated the Frenchwoman at UFC 315 in May 2025. But then, with another title shot within her grasp, Fiorot ran into Grasso, a former champion, at Noche UFC and lost a competitive fight.

9. Erin Blanchfield

UFC flyweight

Previous ranking: 8

Record: 14-2

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Tracy Cortez, Nov. 15, 2025

Next: Oct. 17 vs. Jasmine Jasudavicius

Her rise toward the top of the division was derailed by a March 2024 loss to Manon Fiorot, but Blanchfield bounced back with two straight wins, including one over two-time former strawweight champion Rose Namajunas in November 2024. If she wins her October bout with Jasudavicius, a fellow top-10 flyweight contender, Blanchfield would inch ever closer to a title shot.

10. Tatiana Suarez

UFC strawweight

Previous ranking: 9

Record: 12-1

Last: W (Sub2) vs. Loopy Godínez, April 11

Next: TBA

If Suarez is still feeling the effects of last year's humbling defeat to Zhang Weili in a title challenge, she certainly didn't show it at UFC 327, overcoming early adversity to thrash Godinez, a fellow top-10 strawweight. Suarez is going to be a tough out for anyone at 115 pounds.

stories.headline: Banned Sydney Swans players apologise to AFL club
stories.summary: The five suspended Sydney Swans players have returned to club headquarters for the first time since sexual assault allegations emerged from a post-match party.
stories.body:
Sydney's five suspended players have offered an apology to teammates and colleagues after ending their weeks-long exile from the AFL club.

Swans vice-captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice on Wednesday appeared at Swans HQ for the first time since being banned for breaching club standards in August.

Each individually spoke and apologised to staff and the club's AFL and AFLW playing lists.

Heeney was the only player after the club meeting to address media, doing so with a brief statement.

"It was really nice to address the whole club," he said on Wednesday evening.

"I was thankful they could give us their time and understanding, so yeah, it was really good."

Warner and Bice first arrived together at the club's base at Moore Park, followed by vice-captain Heeney, Blakey and Jordon in the same car.

Only Heeney and Warner spoke to media upon arriving.

Warner, flanked by a silent Bice, said he was "just here for my exit interview".

Asked if he was going to say sorry or anything at all, Warner said: "I don't know."

Heeney did not answer when he was asked if he had a message to fans.

The five have not spoken in public since a club statement was issued following their round 23 match against Essendon in August.

Their club-imposed suspensions are separate from a police investigation into sexual assault allegations.

No charges have been laid, and AAP is not suggesting any wrongdoing on the part of the five suspended players.

All five are contracted for next year, with Blakey signed to the club until 2031.

Warner and Jordon come off contract at the end of 2027, while Heeney and Bice are signed until the end of 2028.

Blakey is reportedly seeking a trade to Victorian rivals, but football boss Leon Cameron had dismissed those rumblings as "speculation" earlier this month.

Victoria Police's eight-week timeline prediction on their investigation into the Pullman Hotel incident - which was first flagged on September 2 - takes in the free agency and trade period from October 2 to October 14.

Main ball-winners Heeney and Warner weren't invited to Monday night's Brownlow Medal at Crown Palladium, but remained eligible for the award.

Heeney and Warner are expected to be frontrunners for Sydney's Bob Skilton Medal, to be held after Saturday's grand final.

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich spoke to reporters earlier on Wednesday and said the club would hear the group out.

"I want them to be themselves," Pavlich said of what he wanted to hear from the players.

"I want them to come in and do what we'd normally do at the end of a season, which is, yeah, player exit meetings.

"If they've got something to say to their player group, if they've got something to say to the club, then we'll hear them out then."

stories.headline: Columbus Crew 2 fires Higuain after fallout from ref abuse
stories.summary: The Columbus Crew announced that Crew 2 manager Federico Higuain has been fired for cause, effective immediately, in the wake of his suspension by MLS NEXT Pro following an incident of misconduct towards a female referee.
stories.body:
The Columbus Crew announced that Crew 2 manager Federico Higuain has been fired for cause, effective immediately, in the wake of his suspension by MLS NEXT Pro following an incident of misconduct towards a female referee.

"We determined it's in the best interest of our Club, players and support staff to dismiss Federico Higuaín from his responsibilities," said Crew General Manager Issa Tall in prepared statement. "After conversations this week and further assessing the past month, our Club's standards of what's expected from a leader for one of our teams have not been met," The Crew's statement added that for the 2026 MLS NEXT Pro Playoffs, the Crew 2 technical staff will assume additional responsibilities ahead of the Club's search for a full-time head coach for the side.

Higuain, 41, was suspended for two games following an Aug. 23 incident that involved him refusing to let go of the hand of a female referee during the post-game handshake, despite being asked three times to do so. Higuain also directed a sexist remark toward the referee saying: "Don't forget that this is a man's game."

Higuain, who excelled as a player for the Crew over eight seasons, was red carded for the incident. In addition to the two-game suspension, Higuain was ordered to undergo restorative practice training, sources told ESPN.

An MLS NEXT Pro spokesperson confirmed that Higuain was suspended for just one additional game, as the policy allows for the red card to count towards the total suspension. The same spokesperson wasn't able to answer the question of why Higuain's actions didn't constitute a forceful grab.

The Professional Soccer Referees Association (PSRA), the union that represents MLS and USL referees, brought the incident to light over the weekend, stating in a social media post that it was not satisfied with the penalties, adding that a "forceful grab" plus the discriminatory language should have been penalized more severely.

While the PSRA's post didn't mention Higuain by name, ESPN reported that the coach in question was Higuain.

"The League's response falls drastically short of the right message to the participants, the referees, and the public. It needs to be reevaluated," the PSRA's social media post read.

The Crew initially issued a statement stating that, "The Crew actively collaborated with MLS NEXT Pro throughout the review process and fully accepted the additional discipline issued in accordance with league policies.

"We condemn any action or notion that contradicts our mission of uniting and uplifting all communities and genders through the global game."

But sources with knowledge of the Crew's decision to fire its coach told ESPN that the club wasn't satisfied with Higuain's response to the incident, saying there was a "lack of contrition" on his part, that he refused to issue a public apology to the female referee, and that there was an overall lack of accountability on the part of its second-team coach.

There was pressure from several of the Crew's supporters groups as well, including the Nordecke and CapyBrava, which both made social media posts demanding that Higuain be fired.

One source said that Higuain was informed of the club's decision early Tuesday afternoon.

In a statement given to ESPN on Sunday, MLS NEXT Pro said the league "immediately investigated the reported incident between the head coach and the female official. It was determined that the coach's behavior violated League policies and warranted additional discipline beyond the red card that was issued in the moment. He served a two-game suspension and is required to participate in a multi-session restorative practices process, which is already underway. The program is intended to support the League's efforts to foster understanding, accountability, respect, and the restoration of relationships across the League. MLS NEXT Pro believes in the restorative approach. The League is confident in its process and the results."

stories.headline: Still at zero: Viral Man United fan's haircut challenge nears two years
stories.summary: Viral Manchester United fan Frank Ilett's haircut challenge is nearing the two-year mark and he's back to square 1.
stories.body:
For most clubs, failure or success can be defined in points, trophies and medals. Manchester United are the same, but they can also define it in days. More specifically, it can be summed up in 712 days.

That's how long viral United fan Frank Ilett, also known as The United Strand, has gone without a haircut as he waits for the team to win five games in a row.

After finishing last season with wins over Nottingham Forest and Brighton, Michael Carrick's side could have completed the job with wins over newly promoted Hull City and Ipswich Town before finishing with a win away at Everton. As it turned out, that's not at all what happened.

An embarrassing 2-0 away defeat to Hull meant going back to square one. A 5-2 win over Ipswich might have promoted hopes that the season opener was just an unwanted blip, but a draw to Everton and a controversial defeat to 10-man Manchester City poured further cold water.

How could it get worse? Well, a 2-0 lead inside the first 10 minutes against Brighton in the Carabao Cup ended in a surprise 3-2 defeat.

Left watching on, his hair growing ever longer, is Ilett. His challenge will now officially reach the two-year mark -- his last haircut was on Oct. 5, 2024 -- and his hair is now almost 14 inches at its longest point.

In the meantime, Ilett continues to raise money for the Little Princess Trust, which creates wigs for children with cancer.

The only thing that can happen now before Ilett soars past two years is for United to win away to Fulham in their last game before the international break.

They appear to have taken note and their defensive work in New Zealand was outstanding. They will need to be at their very best once more against the Roosters, who have the attacking flair to cause them plenty of problems.

The Roosters were simply too good for the Sharks last week, after going very close to beating the Panthers the week before. They have plenty of experience across the park, with Daly Cherry-Evans putting in a much better performance against the Sharks in combination with the hard running Hugo Savala. Outside those two, the Roosters backline bristles with attacking weapons, with Robert Toia and Mark Nawaqanitawase in unstoppable form, James Tedesco always lurking, and Sam Walker returning at halfback.

But, as we all know, the backs don't win the big games, they just determine the score, and the Roosters have a pack that is the match of any in the league. The Knights are playing with the casino's money at this stage. After finishing last in 2025, making the finals surpassed anyone's expectations. stories.headline: Vikings RB Aaron Jones working through knee injury
stories.summary: The Vikings' offensive backfield is in flux this week as starter Aaron Jones Sr. works through a knee injury and backup Jordan Mason remains on injured reserve.
stories.body:
EAGAN, Minn. -- The Minnesota Vikings' offensive backfield is in flux this week as starter Aaron Jones Sr. works through a knee injury and backup Jordan Mason remains on injured reserve.

The team planned to hold Jones out of practice Wednesday, coach Kevin O'Connell said, leaving only one running back on its roster who spent time with the team in training camp: rookie Demond Claiborne. Since then, the Vikings have signed three veterans: DeeJay Dallas, Jerome Ford and Jaret Patterson. As of Wednesday, Ford and Patterson were on the practice squad. Dallas was promoted to the 53-man roster last week.

Jones, 31, is coming off one of his best games in years after carrying 23 times for 105 yards in the Vikings' 9-3 victory over the Chicago Bears. He said afterward that he finished the game while wearing a knee brace. Jones also had a bruise on his left cheek after absorbing a violent hit to the helmet from Bears cornerback Tyrique Stevenson, one that knocked his helmet off.

O'Connell said that Jones feels "pretty good" but gave no indication whether he will be ready to play in the Vikings' game Sunday at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

"We'll just keep getting treatment around the clock," O'Connell said, "and see if we can pick up his workload as the week goes on."

Jones' status is especially notable given the absence of Mason, who fractured his thumb two weeks ago. The Vikings entered the season with Claiborne as their No. 3 back, but he was inactive in Week 1 and got only two snaps in Week 2. Both were pass plays designed for him to get the ball in space. He caught one for 2 yards, and quarterback Carson Wentz scrambled on the other play.

Dallas got two carries and gained 8 yards against the Bears.

stories.headline: 2026 NBA buzz: Latest free agency and trade updates
stories.summary: We're tracking deals, trades and buzz across the NBA, including Pelle Larsson getting a long-term extension with the Heat.
stories.body:
NBA free agency has almost reached the end, with several players landing in new homes this offseason.

LeBron James decided to continue his historic career with the Philadelphia 76ers after months of deliberation. The Sixers also traded for Jaylen Brown this summer, turning the franchise into a true contender with two huge moves.

Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo is headed to South Beach to team up with Bam Adebayo and the Miami Heat, and the Los Angeles Lakers have been sold for the second time in 10 months.

What will happen next during this turbulent offseason?

Check back here for all the latest buzz, news and reactions from our ESPN NBA insiders, with the latest info at the top:

Quick links:

Free agency grades | Trade grades

Trade tracker | Transactions

Depth charts | Trade machine | More

Sept. 23

Extension unlikely as Knicks, Towns talks stall

Talks have stagnated between the New York Knicks and Karl-Anthony Towns on a contract extension, and an agreement is considered unlikely as the team begins training camp next week, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania and Vincent Goodwill on Wednesday.

The sides have spent extensive time discussing a potential extension during the offseason, but there has been no movement lately in negotiations, sources said, as the Knicks stand to go for a repeat following their first NBA title in 53 years.

Sept. 22

Charania: Hield, Nembhard to Charlotte for Finney-Smith
The Atlanta Hawks are trading Dorian Finney-Smith to the Charlotte Hornets for Buddy Hield, Ryan Nembhard and cash, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

Leonard, Raptors agree to two-year extension
The Toronto Raptors and Kawhi Leonard have agreed to a two-year, $115 million extension, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Leonard now has a total of three years and $165 million left on his deal.

The 2026-27 season will be Leonard's first back in Toronto since the 2018-19 campaign, a season in which he helped lead the Raptors to their only title in franchise history.

Sept. 21

Charania: Pistons, Duren at an "impasse"
Free agent center Jalen Duren and the Detroit Pistons are at an impasse this season and the franchise is uncertain if he will show up to next Monday's Media Day, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania.

"When you talk to people close to [Duren], he feels a certain way toward the Pistons' respect level for him," Charania said on NBA Today. "For him it's been all about respect, for the team it has just been about business. ... Over the course of this offseason, his offer has been been around the $180 to $190 million over five years range. And that has also included incentives like weight clauses to my understanding. And that has all played a part in this as well.

"Over the last several weeks it's kind of quiet on this front. The sides have picked up communication. And I am told right now the Pistons offer to Jalen Duren is $200 million over five years."

Duren has until Oct. 1 to sign a qualifying offer.

Hawks' Henri Veesaar out with torn ACL

The Atlanta Hawks announced that center Henri Veesaar tore his ACL during a Sept. 15 workout. He will undergo surgery in October and is expected to miss the entire 2026-27 season.

Sept. 18

Pistons, Thompson reach five-year, $155 million extension
Detroit Pistons All-Defensive forward Ausar Thompson has agreed to a five-year, $155 million rookie-scale contract extension with the franchise, sources told ESPN.

Thompson lands the fully guaranteed extension after making first-team All-Defense and finishing third in Defensive Player of the Year voting last season. The 23-year-old averaged 9.9 points, 5.7 rebounds, 3.1 assists and 0.9 blocks in 2025-26 while leading the NBA in steals per game (2.0).

Heat, Larsson agree to four-year, $60 million extension
Miami Heat guard Pelle Larsson has agreed to a new four-year, $60 million contract extension, with a mutual option for the 2030-31 season, Austin Brown and Steven Heumann of CAA Sports told ESPN on Friday.

A second-round find in the 2024 draft, the 6-foot-5 guard avoids restricted free agency next summer and locks in a new deal with a mutual option that fully guarantees $60 million while allowing either side to opt in on 2030.

Jazz, George agree on a five-year, rookie-scale extension
Utah Jazz guard Keyonte George have agreed on a five-year, $157.5 million rookie-scale contract extension with the franchise, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania and Tim MacMahon. George was the No. 16 pick in the 2023 draft and has averaged 17.2 points and 5.3 assists per game in his three seasons with the Jazz.

Sept. 17

Bey, Pelicans agree to three-year extension
New Orleans Pelicans' Saddiq Bey agreed to a three-year, $55.5 million contract extension with the franchise, plus a trade kicker, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. Bey averaged a career-high 17.7 points per game last season after missing all of the 2024-25 season with a torn ACL.

Sept. 16

Kings remain interested in Duren
The Sacramento Kings continue to loom in the background of Jalen Duren's restricted free agency with the incumbent Detroit Pistons.

Kings general manager Scott Perry met with Duren for dinner in Miami in early July and has maintained a level of steady interest in the ultimate outcome of Duren's free agency, though a path to acquire Duren this summer remains blocked.

Warriors keeping roster spot open for LeBron
The Golden State Warriors enter the second week of July yet to sign an outside free agent.

They were among the group of teams registering a level of interest in veteran wing Rui Hachimura and scoring guard Anfernee Simons, league sources said, but didn't meet the ultimate price point for a contract on either.

Simons went off the board to the Philadelphia 76ers for two years and $12.3 million -- nearly the same contract the Warriors gave to De'Anthony Melton.

They opted to retain Melton instead of putting more behind a pursuit of Simons, team sources said, because of a belief that Melton better fits the backcourt needs of the healthiest version of their current roster. He's not as explosive a scorer but is a more versatile and effective perimeter defender and pairs well with Stephen Curry.

Hachimura's contract terms (two years, $28 million to the LA Clippers) also came in higher than the Warriors proved willing to stretch. They have limited financial flexibility after bringing back Al Horford and Kristaps Porzingis, keeping space for Draymond Green to ultimately return and continuing their slow pursuit of LeBron James.

On the James front, Warriors sources continue to express a low level of optimism that James will ultimately pick them as his next team, but they intend to keep roster space open for James until he ultimately declares his choice. -- Anthony Slater

Expect Monday to be the busiest day on the NBA calendar
Starting at 12:01 p.m. ET, the moratorium will be lifted, meaning the trades that are sending Giannis Antetokounmpo to Miami, Jaylen Brown to Philadelphia, Kawhi Leonard to Toronto and LaMelo Ball to Minnesota can be finalized.

The timeline of trade calls is comparable to waiting on the runway for takeoff. Each trade has a designated time slot for its call, starting early in the afternoon and lasting into the evening. Keep in mind however that players involved in trades must report and pass a physical for a trade to become official.

Trades are not the only transaction that can become official. All player contracts negotiated and agreed upon can be finalized. For example, the Hornets can officially ink Coby White to the three-year, $74 million contract that had been reported.

Teams are also allowed to begin signing players that are extension-eligible. The list of notable players eligible on Monday include Nikola Jokic, Karl-Anthony Towns, Victor Wembanyama, Amen and Ausar Thompson and Cason Wallace. Donovan Mitchell is eligible starting Tuesday.

One more item to watch is restricted free agents, notably Peyton Watson and Jalen Duren.

If either player signs an offer sheet prior to noon ET, his prior team will have until 11:59 p.m. ET on July 7 to match. If the offer sheet comes in after noon ET, his prior team has until 1:59 p.m. ET on July 8 to match. -- Bobby Marks

Why Dolan is so worried about the second apron
The New York Knicks' championship parade has not even started, but there are already questions over whether finances will break up the roster.

"If we could bring back the whole team, exactly as is, why wouldn't you?" Knicks owner James Dolan said Wednesday on WFAN's "Carton Show." "I don't know if we'll be able to.

"We're willing to stretch, but there's certain things in the NBA that you'd have to be suicidal to do. One of them is the second apron. Cannot go into the second apron."

Including the 24th pick in next week's draft (June 23 and 24, 8 p.m. ET on ABC/ESPN), New York is $13 million below the second apron and has decisions with free agents Landry Shamet, Mitchell Robinson and possibly Jose Alvarado. (Alvarado has until Monday to decide on his $4.5 million option.) The entire starting five, meanwhile, is under contract through at least 2026-27. Karl-Anthony Towns is extension-eligible this summer and can become a free agent in the 2027 offseason if an agreement is not reached.

The second apron is a punitive luxury tax threshold restricting how teams add to their rosters in free agency, trades and the draft. In the case of the Knicks, the team would not be allowed to send cash in a trade, use the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception, aggregate salaries in a trade or use more than 100% of the traded player exception.

A team cannot trade its first-round pick seven years out if it finishes over the second apron in consecutive seasons, which no team has ever done. That same pick could be moved back to the end of the first round if a team finishes over the second apron in three out of four seasons. Luckily for Dolan and the Knicks, there are no rules that prohibit a team from retaining its own players.

New York can exceed the threshold to sign Robinson, Shamet and Alvarado. If the Knicks let the three players sign elsewhere, they would have their first-round pick (New York also has the 31st and 55th picks in the second round), the $6.1 million tax midlevel exception and $2.5 million veteran minimum exceptions available as replacements.

Since the apron rules were implemented before the 2024-25 season, Cleveland, Phoenix, Minnesota and Boston have finished the regular season over the second apron. The Knicks finished the past two seasons $53,000 and $370,000 below. Next offseason, New York is projected to be $31 million below the second apron with seven players under contract. -- Bobby Marks

The NBA retroactively assessed Charlotte Hornets guard LaMelo Ball with a flagrant foul 2 for tripping Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo in Tuesday's Eastern Conference play-in game, which Charlotte won in overtime thanks to Ball's last-second layup.

The NBA's take on tanking

ESPN's Anthony Slater talked to players, coaches and executives about how they feel about tanking in the NBA and the future it has in the league.

In ESPN's conversations with dozens of players, coaches and front office executives, a consistent theme emerged: Nobody likes it -- "I hate it," Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said -- but not many deny it is often the most prudent team-building path when stuck near the bottom. Different seasons and different drafts will generate different forms, but everyone agrees it'll continue until the NBA figures out either the proper rules or punishments to curb it.

"These teams are doing the whole gamut: sitting guys in the fourth, playing analytically bad lineups, drawing up plays for bad shots," one Western Conference general manager said. "The creativity is impressive and I don't blame them. It's the best strategy to get better. Look at all the most promising teams in the league: Thunder, Spurs, Pistons, Rockets, Hornets. Years of being bad and building up on high picks. It's painful but worthwhile."

The strategies are growing in audaciousness and frequency of use. The orders from management are coming in earlier in the season, creating months of competitively compromised and often unwatchable basketball. The average margin of victory in NBA games this season is 13.1 points, the largest spread in history, and a record 89 games have been decided by 30 or more points.

The Chicago Bulls are expected to engage a search firm in order to find a replacement for vice president Arturas Karnisovas and general manager Marc Eversley, whom the team fired after six seasons running the basketball operations department, sources told ESPN.

It's a different approach from the process Chicago used when it hired Karnisovas in 2020. Team president and CEO Michael Resindorf said then that he targeted the top "No. 2" in basketball and went after general managers such as Karnisovas, who was then with the Denver Nuggets, and Bobby Webster, who was then general manager of the Toronto Raptors, but has since been promoted to their head of basketball operations.

This is only the second time since 2003 that the Bulls have hired a new head of basketball operations. Before Karnisovas got the job in 2020, John Paxson assumed the role for 17 years from 2003 to '20. Karnisovas and Eversley went 224-254 across six seasons leading the organization to one winning season and one playoff appearance.

Even though Chicago sits 29-49 and in 12th place in the Eastern Conference, the opening is expected to be an attractive one around the league. All the while, the uncertainty of Antetokounmpo's future in Milwaukee lingered. The Bucks engaged in trade talks ahead of the Feb. 5 trade deadline but chose to hold on to him, even as it became increasingly clear that they didn't have much hope of even elevating into the play-in race. Milwaukee is now headed to the draft lottery for the first time since 2016, snapping a streak of nine consecutive years in the playoffs. The Bucks haven't won a postseason series since 2022. Antetokounmpo, who is under contract for one more season, has played in a career-low 36 games and privately feuded with the organization for several months, culminating in rebuking the team's requests to shut down in the final month of the season and setting up another contentious summer.

The Bucks have officially been eliminated from the playoffs.

Doncic signed a three-year extension last August and has been named All-NBA in five of the six previous seasons.

There will be no financial implications in his next contract if the application is denied.

Though the Lakers haven't provided a timeline for his return, Grade 2 hamstring injuries typically require a monthlong recovery. Doncic has averaged a league-high 33.5 points this season, along with 7.7 rebounds and 8.3 assists.

stories.headline: Alpine's Pierre Gasly warns against 'disturbing' threats after teammate Franco Colapinto incident
stories.summary: Pierre Gasly has hit out at the "disturbing" threats he, his girlfriend and his family received after he held up Argentine teammate Franco Colapinto in the closing stages of the Spanish Grand Prix two weeks ago.
stories.body:
Pierre Gasly has hit out at the "disturbing" threats he, his girlfriend and his family received after he held up Argentine teammate Franco Colapinto in the closing stages of the Spanish Grand Prix two weeks ago.

Late in the Madring contest, Gasly appeared to get in the way of his Alpine teammate before making a pit stop.

The time loss left Colapinto vulnerable to the chasing McLaren of Oscar Piastri, and he complained about Gasly several times on the radio, although he was ultimately able to hold on to seventh position.

Gasly said the abuse crossed a line.

"Personally, I find it a little bit disturbing for our sport," Gasly is reported by The Race as saying during media day for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

"I'm a top athlete, so I know I'm exposed, it's always been the case, but the extent of the threats, attacks, I find completely inappropriate, especially when it reaches out to family members, [my] girlfriend etc. I don't think that should be the case.

"Things were not that way in the past and as a sport we just need to find a way to make it a healthier place because you're exposed, you know you are going to be attacked.

"You can be liked, disliked, it's completely fine, but there is a certain line that should not be crossed just because you're behind a screen and a keyboard, and these lines are crossed too many times."

- Isack Hadjar expects wrist injury to 'still be painful' on Azerbaijan Grand Prix return

- Why is the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on a Saturday, not a Sunday? Baku schedule shift explained

- Haas' Esteban Ocon future in F1 unclear: 'Free agent' for 2027 season

Fan abuse has been a regular story when it comes to incidents involving Colapinto, who has become an Argentine sporting hero since his debut in 2024.

FIA race stewards were bombarded with abuse after Colapinto received a penalty at last month's Dutch Grand Prix, while Alpine have had to condemn death threats aimed at Esteban Ocon after the Chinese Grand Prix and at Yuki Tsunoda after last year's Emilia-Romagna Grand Prix.

Australian driver Jack Doohan, whom Colapinto replaced at Alpine in 2025, had to ask the Argentine's fans to "stop harassing my family" last year.

Doohan later revealed he had "six or seven threatening emails that all my limbs would be cut off" if he was still driving instead of Colapinto at that year's Miami Grand Prix, which prompted police intervention.

It has not just been one-way. Alpine publicly condemned social media abuse aimed at Colapinto in April this year, as well as dismissing the "completely unfounded" suggestion that they were sabotaging the Argentine driver in favour of Gasly.

Speaking on Wednesday, Colapinto stressed that he and Gasly have a good relationship and said he hopes to see the abuse stop in future.

"I think he got a lot of people messaging him," Colapinto said on the subject of Gasly's abuse. "I haven't seen it because I'm not on social media a lot, but it's never nice to get it, even more when it's happening to the team that I'm racing in.

"We are team-mates and we get on very well together. We are playing and focusing on the same result, and [have] the same goal and the same target -- that is to make Alpine better. We are always working as a team and it's not nice to see it.

"So, hopefully, they can stop it. The same happened to other drivers -- Yuki [Tsunoda] last year, it was quite bad as well at one point, I talked about it.

"The stewards, after Zandvoort, I went to see them as well. They had some abuse after the penalty they gave me. It happens a lot with fans in Formula 1, in any sport nowadays, it's something very common.

"Unfortunately, that shouldn't be common. Definitely, we should be taking more care about the things, the words that come out of the keyboards of everyone."

He added: "Hopefully, it doesn't keep happening. But it's something tricky with fans in the sport. It's not just my fans. I've got some very passionate ones. They want me to do well. Hopefully, they can enjoy the good results I'm having."

stories.headline: Bounce-back picks: The fantasy hockey stars looking to turn back the clock
stories.summary: Here are the fantasy hockey players poised to return to past success, and others you should be wary of.
stories.body:
Even Connor McDavid has a down year in him.

In 2024-25, the best player alive slipped from 3.21 fantasy points per game (FPPG) the year prior to 2.60, the kind of "collapse" that would be a career year for almost anyone else. Then he did what the genuinely elite tend to do after a dip: climbed right back to 3.21. If it can happen to McDavid, it can happen to whichever name on your roster you spent last spring apologizing for.

That's the whole bounceback game; separating the skaters who are actually declining from the ones who just caught a bad hand of variance, injuries or linemate roulette, and are now sitting a round or two cheaper than they should be because of it.

Going back to 2009-10, 59 forwards clearing a career mark of 1.7 FPPG have suffered a real down season -- a drop of 0.35 FPPG or more -- and later climbed back above their career average, a feat they pulled off 78 times between them. Some made a career of it: Evgeni Malkin bounced back four separate times, Matt Duchene an almost comical five. The blue line tells the same story, just rarer -- 20 defenders have done it off that same 1.7 bar, with Kris Letang, Roman Josi, Ryan Pulock and Shayne Gostisbehere each rebounding twice. Fewer names, which is exactly why a bouncing-back defender is worth chasing: the position is thin enough that buying one back at a discount can swing your whole season.

And you don't need the archives for proof. Last season alone, Jason Robertson, Mikko Rantanen, Mika Zibanejad and Zach Hyman shook off ugly 2024-25 campaigns up front, while Charlie McAvoy, Adam Fox, Noah Dobson and Brock Faber did the exact same on the back end. Every one of them rewarded whoever drafted them at a discount.

Not every name below carries that 1.7 pedigree, a few are cheaper bets where a bad year has buried a genuinely useful player, but the shape is identical. Down season, recovery profile, discount at the table. Because this is about fantasy value, period, not star power.

So don't overthink the down year. Below are the forwards and defense primed for a possible return to value with a verdict on whether I think the dip is an opportunity or an obituary.

More: Sign up for free | Rankings | Projections | League types

Bounce-back forwards

Auston Matthews, C, Toronto Maple Leafs (29.0 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 2.89/2.98/2.56): The offense stalled without Mitch Marner. Starved of setups, Matthews opened with just 15 goals in the first three months, ranking a very un-Matthews-like 38th in the league. He later endured a stretch of 12 games with no goals before finally scoring in the same game that Radko Gudas ended his season early. The end result was a season capped at 60 games (27 goals, 53 points). But the finish still plays -- he was sixth in the league in shots per minute -- and if Gavin McKenna even partly fills the Marner void, the setups return and the knee is the only thing that has to heal.

Verdict: A clean yes. Matthews is a Rocket Richard-threat at a discount because of a lost year. Just confirm the knee checks out at camp. If it does, don't let him slip out of the first round.

Mitch Marner, RW, Vegas Golden Knights (29.3 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 2.20/2.33/1.96): Year 1 in Vegas was a soft landing, not a letdown, as he drove a line all season and then led the entire NHL in playoff scoring once it counted. He settles in beside William Karlsson on the second line and onto a dangerous power play that has minutes to spare now that Pavel Dorofeyev is gone. Losing Dorofeyev's finishing touch is a concern, not a dealbreaker. Marner will find a new muse.

Verdict: The question is whether he'll be good or trend back toward great. Luckily, the floor on Marner is still a top-50 forward, so it's not as if there is much downside to banking on a bigger season.

J.T. Miller, C/LW, New York Rangers (33.5 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.92/2.23/1.82): His first full season back in New York was swallowed by injuries and a team-wide scoring drought, but he found his game in the second half and posted fantasy relevant totals in March and April. With Vincent Trocheck traded to Utah, Miller is finally locked into the full-time center role he prefers behind Mika Zibanejad instead of shuffling to the wing.

Verdict: Role clarity plus health makes him a strong middle-rounds target. He's 33, so don't chase the peak, but 70-plus points is very much on the table.

Brayden Point, C/RW, Tampa Bay Lightning (30.5 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 2.08/2.38/1.57): The bet here is murkier than it looks. Point missed 19 games and his counting stats cratered -- 18 goals, a career-low 14.0 shooting percentage -- but he waved off injuries as the cause at season's end, saying instead that his game has to evolve as he ages. That's honest, and a little worrying: a healthy-but-declining 30-year-old is a different draft proposition than a hurt one bouncing back. Counterpoint, he's still centering Nikita Kucherov and Jake Guentzel on a top power play, so the setups and volume are there if the finish returns.

Verdict: A calculated gamble, not a slam-dunk yes. The talent and linemates argue for a rebound, as his own words argue caution. Fine as a mid-round dart if he slips - but don't pay for the 40-goal ceiling on faith.

Jesper Bratt, RW, New Jersey Devils (28.1 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.70/2.18/1.73): He didn't decline so much as shed 14 points of power-play production and some of Jack Hughes' availability, though the even-strength chemistry with Hughes never went anywhere. With Hughes healthy, the scoring should climb. The wrinkle is the power play: New Jersey added top-six wing depth this offseason without subtracting any, so Bratt's man-advantage looks aren't the lock they were. He has to earn the PP1 time that drove his best years, not inherit it.

Verdict: A rebound bet with a catch. Healthy Hughes lifts his even-strength floor, but the crowded forward group puts his power-play ceiling in play, and the PP is where his upside lives.

Nazem Kadri, C/LW, Colorado Avalanche (35.9 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.70/1.95/1.52): The down year was a slog on a bad Calgary team plus a deadline move, and the Colorado reunion hands him far better company to keep. The catch is the depth chart: he projects behind Nathan MacKinnon and Brock Nelson at center, so his ceiling hinges on top-six looks and power-play time.

Verdict: The environment upgrade is real, but temper it. Take him as a mid-round multi-category center, not a star. If coach Jared Bednar commits him to a scoring role, the 20-goal, 60-point version is back.

Tomas Hertl, C, Vegas Golden Knights (32.8 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.80/2.19/1.81): He slid back to about his career rate, and the real drag is depth-chart gravity. In Vegas's loaded top nine, he's the third-line center behind Jack Eichel and William Karlsson. What rescues his value is the power play, where he's locked onto the top unit.

Verdict: A quietly reliable rebound driven almost entirely by PP1. He won't win your league, but he'll out-earn his cost; grab him once the top center tiers clear.

Dylan Strome, C, Washington Capitals (29.5 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.64/2.10/1.62): He's still Washington's top-line pivot, but everything cooled at once last year. Those are classic bounce-back signals, and the Capitals added Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch to deepen the scoring around him, and they might even end up flanking him full-time.

Verdict: A textbook draft-low: same premium role, colder-than-real results. Target him in the middle rounds and expect a return to the 70-point neighborhood.

Jordan Kyrou, RW, Washington Capitals (28.3 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.69/1.97/1.44): A trade to Washington is a fresh start after his shooting percentage bottomed out, but the shot volume never did. He ranked 31st in the league in shots per 60 last season, right in the mix with names like Kirill Kaprizov and Kyle Connor, so the finishing slump reads as variance, not decline. He arrives a three-time 30-goal scorer built for sheltered, offensive-zone minutes, whether he lines up with Pierre-Luc Dubois or slots up alongside Strome.

Verdict: Believe the goal rebound with one caveat -- the top power-play spot is a rotation, so his special-teams points aren't locked. A mid-round price for a run back at 30 goals is worth it.

Valeri Nichushkin, RW, Columbus Blue Jackets (31.5 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.42/2.02/1.44): He lands in Columbus off a down year, and the draw is real: he ranked 28th in the NHL in goals per game over the four seasons prior to falling off. The knocks are real, too, though: he only played 212 of the 328 games in those four years, and Columbus is jammed with middle-six forwards fighting for the same minutes.

Verdict: A boom-or-bust multi-category flier. If he wins a top-six job and stays on the ice, the draft spot is a steal. Take him late and be ready to move on if the role wavers.

John Tavares, C, Toronto Maple Leafs (36.0 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 2.11/2.31/1.84): The production didn't just dip, it fell off his own career pace, from 2.31 the year before to 1.84, his leanest full season in years. But the role that made him useful is intact: he anchors a second line with William Nylander, remains a power-play fixture and still gets his net-front goals. At 36 the age is real, but a half-point below his career rate is steeper than his usage says it should be.

Verdict: A modest bounce-back on role alone - the Nylander line and power-play time argue the 1.84 was low, not the new normal.

Alex Ovechkin, LW/RW, Washington Capitals (41.0 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 2.61/2.60/1.85): Even at 41 he led Washington in goals and didn't miss a game. The collapse was specifically on the power play, where his shooting percentage fell off a cliff (a career-low five power-play goals) while the unit kept generating chances at his usual rate. He still owns a top power-play role, and the Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch additions should feed the setups.

Verdict: The volume and PP1 real estate make a goal rebound likely; believe in the shot totals and expect the man-advantage finishing to normalize - just don't expect that 2024-25 magic to return.

Made it this far? Create your own league with your own rules and play against your friends today.

Bounce-back defense

MacKenzie Weegar, D, Utah Mammoth (32.7 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.93/2.51/1.96): His rate dipped thanks to the fantasy void of Calgary and the deeper Utah blue line after he was traded, but he eventually settled in next to Mikhail Sergachev on the top pair and looked the part by the postseason. He's a true multi-category starter, as he finished the past three seasons ranked second or third in the league in fantasy points from hits and blocked shots combined.

Verdict: A solid rebound with one ceiling-cap: Sergachev runs the top power play, so Weegar's points lean even-strength. He can still be a No. 2 defender for fantasy thanks to his elite peripherals.

Shea Theodore, D, Vegas Golden Knights (31.1 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.73/1.91/1.54): His power-play value slipped when Vegas leaned on a five-forward attack most nights. And when they did run a defenseman up top, the job stopped being his alone. After Rasmus Andersson arrived at the deadline, the two split the blue line's power-play minutes almost evenly across the games they both dressed. Theodore led on some nights, Andersson on others, and on a couple even Noah Hanifin topped them both. The PP1 role went from Theodore's to a committee.

Verdict: Don't draft Theodore as a lock for power-play quarterback minutes. He'll get them if Vegas backs off the five-forward look, but he has to hold off a legitimate top-pair talent in Andersson, and last year the split was closer to even than settled.

Colton Parayko, D, St. Louis Blues (33.3 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 1.83/2.34/1.66): His ceiling season was inflated by a shooting percentage twice his career norm, and last year's slide came with back and knee trouble plus a more purely defensive assignment. The peripherals are dependable, like top-pair minutes, penalty-kill time and 160-plus blocks.

Verdict: Expect a multi-category floor, not a goal repeat, because the 16-goal spike isn't the baseline. A late-round blocks-and-shots defender who's far more valuable in banger and category leagues than points-only.

Victor Hedman, D, Tampa Bay Lightning (35.7 years old, FPPG career/2024-25/last season 2.06/2.31/1.51): His down year came with the season ending early when he stepped away from the team for personal reasons, not from any erosion of his game. The complication for 2026-27 is new arrival John Carlson, who projects onto the top unit and could split the power-play quarterback minutes.

Verdict: Let someone else pay for the name. The talent still says rebound if he's back and right, but that's the problem. It's one "if" stacked on two more: he turns 36 this season and Carlson's arrival threatens power-play minutes. Any one of those is manageable; all three at a Hedman price is a pick you don't need to make.
